1:1: The word Qoheleth is the name that the main speaker of this book chose to use for himself. In the original language it is a title that means “one who assembles a group,” that is, someone who gathers people together in order to teach them.
1:2: Qoheleth is using Vapor of vapors as a common expression of his culture to mean “the most fleeting thing of all.” In this expression, a word is repeated in the possessive form in order to express a superlative.
Qoheleth says the whole as an extreme statement for emphasis. He does not mean that every single thing without exception is fleeting.
1:3: מַה יִּתְרוֹן לָאָדָם בְּכָל עֲמָלוֹ שֶׁיַּעֲמֹל תַּחַת הַשָּׁמֶשׁ
Qoheleth is not using the question form to emphasize that people gain nothing lasting from all their labor. Instead, this is a genuine question.
Qoheleth is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root.
See the Introduction to Ecclesiastes for more information on translating this expression here and throughout this chapter.
1:4: Qoheleth is referring to the whole cycle of human life by naming its two major components, one generation going and another generation coming.
1:5: Qoheleth is speaking of the sun as if it were a living thing that could be panting as it hurried back to the place where it rises.
1:6: Qoheleth is referring to all directions by naming two major components, south and north.
הוֹלֵךְ הָרוּחַ וְעַל סְבִיבֹתָיו שָׁב הָרוּחַ
Qoheleth is speaking of the wind as if it were a living thing that could choose where to travel and then decide to return the same way.
1:8: Qoheleth says All the things are wearisome and a person is not able to speak as extreme statements for emphasis. He means that the endless repetition he has been describing is exhausting to consider and that no one could ever finish describing how wearisome these things are.
לֹא תִשְׂבַּע עַיִן לִרְאוֹת וְלֹא תִמָּלֵא אֹזֶן מִשְּׁמֹעַ
These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words.
1:10: יֵשׁ דָּבָר שֶׁיֹּאמַר רְאֵה זֶה חָדָשׁ הוּא
Qoheleth is using the question form to make an emphatic statement, that nothing anyone points to is actually new.
Here, our faces represents “us,” that is, the people who are alive now.
1:11: Qoheleth is referring to people and events of every time by naming two major components, the former times and the latter times.
1:13: The terms to seek and to explore mean similar things. Qoheleth is using the two terms together for emphasis, indicating that his investigation was thorough.
Qoheleth is using under the heavens as a common expression of his culture to mean “in this life on the earth.” This expression means the same thing as “under the sun” in 1:3.
1:14: Qoheleth is using the term behold to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say.
Qoheleth is speaking of everything people do as if it were a pursuit of wind. He means that gaining anything lasting from these deeds is as futile as trying to catch the wind.
1:15: Qoheleth is speaking of what is wrong in the world as if it were a bent object that someone might try to make straight. He means that people cannot correct the things that are wrong with life.
1:16: Here, my face represents Qoheleth speaking of himself.

Qoheleth is speaking of his heart as if it were a person who could see. In this culture, the heart represented a person’s thoughts and understanding, and seeing something represented experiencing and knowing it.
The terms wisdom and knowledge mean similar things. Qoheleth is using the two terms together for emphasis.
2:1: Qoheleth is speaking of his own thoughts as if they were a person that he could talk to, his heart.
Qoheleth is speaking of good as if it were a thing that he could see.
Qoheleth is using the term behold to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say.
Qoheleth is speaking of the pleasure he had experienced as if it were vapor, that is, something as fleeting and insubstantial as a puff of breath.
2:2: Qoheleth is speaking To laughter and to joy though he knows they cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening that he feels very strongly about these emotions and their place in life.
Qoheleth is using the question form to show that pleasure accomplishes nothing worthwhile.
2:3: Qoheleth is speaking of his heart as if it were a living thing that could guide him.
Qoheleth is speaking of folly as if it were an object that he could take hold of with his hand.
2:4: בָּנִיתִי לִי בָּתִּים נָטַעְתִּי לִי כְּרָמִים
Qoheleth is using I built for myself houses and I planted for myself vineyards to represent the work that he had others do for him.
2:5: The term royal parks describes large, enclosed gardens that belonged to a king.
2:7: Here the expression to my face means “before me” (in time).
2:8: Qoheleth is using breast and breasts to represent women.
2:9: Qoheleth is speaking of his wisdom as if it were a living thing that could stand beside him as a companion.
2:10: Qoheleth is speaking of the enjoyment that he received from his work as if it were a portion of land or food that had been assigned to him.
2:11: Here, my hands represents my own efforts.
Qoheleth is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root.
2:12: Qoheleth is using the question form to emphasize that whoever comes after him will not be able to do anything more than what has already been done.
2:13: The point of this comparison is that just as the light is more useful than the darkness for seeing where one is going, so wisdom is more useful than folly for living well.
2:14: Qoheleth is speaking of the way a foolish person lives as if it were walking in the darkness.
Qoheleth is using a construction in which a verb and its subject come from the same root.
The implication is that the one happening that will happen to both of them is death.
2:15: Qoheleth is using the question form to express his frustration that becoming wise gained him no lasting advantage.
2:18: אֶת כָּל עֲמָלִי שֶׁאֲנִי עָמֵל תַּחַת הַשָּׁמֶשׁ
Here, my toil represents what I had gained by my toil.
2:19: וּמִי יוֹדֵעַ הֶחָכָם יִהְיֶה אוֹ סָכָל
Qoheleth is using the question form to emphasize that no one is able to know the answer.
2:22: Qoheleth is using the question form to emphasize that nothing lasting comes to a person from all his hard work.
2:23: Qoheleth is speaking of a person’s days as if they were pains and of his anger as if it were business.
2:24: Here, the hand of the God represents what God gives.
2:25: כִּי מִי יֹאכַל וּמִי יָחוּשׁ חוּץ מִמֶּנִּי
Qoheleth is using the question form to emphasize that no one is able to eat or to enjoy anything apart from God.
2:26: Here, to his face represents in his judgment.
The terms gathering and collecting mean similar things. Qoheleth is using the two terms together for emphasis.
3:9: Solomon is using the question form to emphasize that there is no profit for the worker.
3:11: Here Solomon is speaking as if the inner being of a person were their heart.
Solomon is referring to all of God’s work in its entirety by naming two major components, beginning and end.
3:14: עָלָיו אֵין לְהוֹסִיף וּמִמֶּנּוּ אֵין לִגְרֹעַ
Qoheleth is referring to all possible changes by naming two major components, nothing to add and nothing to remove.
3:16: מְקוֹם הַמִּשְׁפָּט שָׁמָּה הָרֶשַׁע וּמְקוֹם הַצֶּדֶק שָׁמָּה הָרָשַׁע
These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words.
3:18: Here Solomon is speaking as if human beings were animals. He means that in terms of mortality, humans are no different from animals.
3:20: Qoheleth is referring to death in a polite way by using the phrase going to one place.
הַכֹּל הָיָה מִן־הֶעָפָר וְהַכֹּל שָׁב אֶל־הֶעָפָר
Here Qoheleth is speaking as if people and animals were made from the dust and will become dust again. He is alluding to the way God created the first human being out of the ground.
3:21: Qoheleth is using the question form to express that no one can know for certain what happens after death.
3:22: Here Qoheleth is speaking as if the enjoyment of work were a portion of food allotted to someone. He means that it is what God has assigned to each person.
כִּי מִי יְבִיאֶנּוּ לִרְאוֹת בְּמֶה שֶׁיִּהְיֶה אַחֲרָיו
Qoheleth is using the question form to emphasize that no one can show a person what will happen after him.
4:1: Qoheleth says all the oppressions as an extreme statement for emphasis. He means very many oppressions, not necessarily every single one.
Qoheleth is using the term behold to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say.
Here, the tears of the oppressed represents their grief and suffering.
Here, the hand represents the power or control of the ones oppressing them.
4:4: אֶת כָּל עָמָל וְאֵת כָּל כִּשְׁרוֹן הַמַּעֲשֶׂה
The terms every toil and every success of the deed mean similar things. Solomon is using the two terms together for emphasis.
4:5: הַכְּסִיל חֹבֵק אֶת יָדָיו וְאֹכֵל אֶת בְּשָׂרוֹ
Qoheleth uses a proverb in order to illustrate the self-destructive nature of laziness.
Qoheleth is speaking as if the fool’s laziness were causing him to consume his own flesh. He means that the fool’s idleness destroys himself.
4:6: Qoheleth uses a proverb in order to teach that contentment with little is better than striving for much.
Qoheleth is speaking as if having a small amount with peace were having a fullness of a palm with quiet. He means that having few possessions and being content is valuable.
4:8: Here, his eye represents his desire or appetite.
וּלְמִי אֲנִי עָמֵל וּמְחַסֵּר אֶת נַפְשִׁי מִטּוֹבָה
The lonely person is using the question form to emphasize that there is no good reason for his solitary toil.
Here, my soul represents the person himself.
4:12: Qoheleth is speaking as if the bond between three people were a three-fold rope that cannot easily be torn in two. He means that three people united together are very strong.
4:13: טוֹב יֶלֶד מִסְכֵּן וְחָכָם מִמֶּלֶךְ זָקֵן וּכְסִיל
Qoheleth uses a proverb in order to teach that wisdom is more valuable than power or age.
4:16: Qoheleth says There was no end to all the people as an extreme statement for emphasis. He means that there were very many people.
5:1: Here Qoheleth is speaking as if the temple were the house of God, since that was the place where God made his presence known among his people.
5:2: Here, your mouth represents what you say.
Here Qoheleth is speaking as if your thoughts and intentions were your heart.
Here, to the face of God represents being in the presence of God.
כִּי הָאֱלֹהִים בַּשָּׁמַיִם וְאַתָּה עַל הָאָרֶץ
The implication is that God is exalted far above people and so should be addressed with reverence and with few words.
5:3: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words.
Here, the voice of a fool represents what a fool says.
5:4: Qoheleth is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root.
The implication is that it is God who has no delight in fools who do not fulfill what they have vowed.
5:6: Qoheleth is using your flesh to represent your whole self.
The phrase the messenger could mean: (1) the priest who came to collect what a person had vowed to give to God; or (2) an angel sent by God.
5:7: Here Qoheleth is speaking as if things that are empty and fleeting were vaporous things.
5:8: The phrase justice and equity expresses a single idea. The word equity tells more about justice.
The phrase for a high one over a high one is watching could mean: (1) that each official is protected by another official who is more powerful than he is; or (2) that God watches over all of them.
5:9: The implication is that even a king depends on what farmland produces, although it is also possible that Solomon means that a king who promotes farming benefits everyone in his land.
5:11: Here Qoheleth is speaking as if using up a person’s wealth were eating it.
וּמַה כִּשְׁרוֹן לִבְעָלֶיהָ כִּי אִם ראית עֵינָיו
Qoheleth is using the question form to emphasize that the owner of such wealth gains no real advantage from it.
5:12: Here Qoheleth is speaking as if restful and satisfying sleep were Sweet.
Qoheleth is referring to all the amounts that a worker might eat by naming two major components, however little and however much.
וְהַשָּׂבָע לֶעָשִׁיר אֵינֶנּוּ מַנִּיחַ לוֹ לִישׁוֹן
Qoheleth is speaking of the satisfaction of a rich person as if it were a living thing that could keep him from sleeping.
5:13: Here Qoheleth is speaking as if the misfortune that he saw were a disease, calling it sickening.
5:14: The implication is that this man had nothing left to leave to his son.
Here, in his hand represents in his possession.
5:15: Qoheleth is referring to dying in a polite way by using the phrase he will go again.
Qoheleth is using naked, which describes a person who has no clothing, to represent a person who has no possessions at all.
5:16: Qoheleth is using the question form to emphasize that such a person gains nothing at all from his work.
Here Qoheleth is speaking as if the results of such a person’s work were the wind.
5:17: Here Qoheleth is speaking as if the gloom and misery in which such a person lives were darkness.
5:18: Qoheleth is using the term Behold to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say.
5:19: וְהִשְׁלִיטוֹ לֶאֱכֹל מִמֶּנּוּ וְלָשֵׂאת אֶת חֶלְקוֹ וְלִשְׂמֹחַ בַּעֲמָלוֹ
The implication is that the ability to enjoy wealth is itself a gift that God must give, since not everyone whom God makes wealthy is able to enjoy what he has.
5:20: כִּי לֹא הַרְבֵּה יִזְכֹּר אֶת יְמֵי חַיָּיו
The implication is that such a person does not brood over how short and troubled his life is.
Here Qoheleth is speaking as if a person’s inner feelings were his heart.
6:2: לֶאֱכֹל מִמֶּנּוּ כִּי אִישׁ נָכְרִי יֹאכֲלֶנּוּ
Here Qoheleth is speaking as if the wealth that God gives were food that a person could eat.
Here Qoheleth is speaking as if this situation were vapor, which appears for a moment and then is gone. This also occurs in verse 9.
6:3: Qoheleth says a hundred children as an extreme statement for emphasis.
וְשָׁנִים רַבּוֹת יִחְיֶה וְרַב ׀ שֶׁיִּהְיוּ יְמֵי־שָׁנָיו
These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words.
This could mean: (1) that this man does not receive an honorable burial, which was a great disgrace in this culture; or (2) that he lives forever and so does not need to be buried.
6:4: Qoheleth is referring to being born and dying in a polite way by using the phrase in vapor it came, and in the darkness it will go.
Here Qoheleth is speaking as if the child’s name were an object that the darkness hides from sight. He means that no one ever remembers this child.
6:6: Qoheleth says And if he lived a thousand years twice to introduce an imaginary situation to help explain that even a very long life has no value if a person does not enjoy it.
Qoheleth says a thousand years twice as an extreme statement for emphasis.
Qoheleth is using the question form to emphasize that every person dies, no matter how long he lives.
Qoheleth is referring to dying in a polite way by using the phrase going to one place.
6:7: כָּל־עֲמַל הָאָדָם לְפִיהוּ וְגַם־הַנֶּפֶשׁ לֹא תִמָּלֵא
Qoheleth uses or invents a proverb in order to show that people work only to satisfy their appetites and yet are never satisfied.
Here, his mouth represents the food that he eats.
Here, the soul represents the appetite, not the spirit.
6:8: Qoheleth is using the question form to emphasize that a wise person has no lasting advantage over a foolish person.
Qoheleth is using the question form to emphasize that a poor person who knows how to conduct himself well gains no lasting advantage either.
6:9: Qoheleth uses or invents a proverb in order to teach that being content with what a person already has is better than craving what he does not have.
6:10: The implication is that he who is more powerful than him is God.
6:11: Qoheleth is using the question form to emphasize that speaking many words brings no benefit to people.
6:12: כִּי מִי־יוֹדֵעַ מַה־טּוֹב לָאָדָם בַּחַיִּים מִסְפַּר יְמֵי־חַיֵּי הֶבְלוֹ
Qoheleth is using the question form to emphasize that no one knows what is good for a person to do during his brief life.
The point of this comparison is that just as the shadow is brief and quickly gone, so are the days of a person’s life.
אֲשֶׁר מִי־יַגִּיד לָאָדָם מַה־יִּהְיֶה אַחֲרָיו תַּחַת הַשָּׁמֶשׁ
Qoheleth is using the question form to emphasize that no one is able to tell a person what will happen after he dies.
Here, what will be after him could mean: (1) what will happen after he dies; or (2) what will happen to him later in life.
7:1: Here Qoheleth uses or invents a proverb in order to teach that what people remember about a person is worth more than what money can buy.
The implication is that good oil is expensive perfumed oil, which people in this culture valued highly.
7:2: Here, a house of mourning and a house of a banquet represent the gatherings that people hold in those places.
Qoheleth is referring to dying in a polite way by using the phrase the end of all humanity.
7:3: Here Qoheleth is speaking as if a person’s inner self were his heart.
7:4: Here Qoheleth is speaking as if the thoughts and inclinations of wise people were their heart, which could be in a place.
7:5: The implication is that a song of fools is entertainment and flattery that pleases a person but teaches him nothing.
7:6: כְקוֹל הַסִּירִים תַּחַת הַסִּיר כֵּן שְׂחֹק הַכְּסִיל
The point of this comparison is that just as the sound of the thorns under the cooking-pot is loud but produces almost no heat, so is the laughter of the fool loud but worth nothing.
Qoheleth is using words with similar sounds for poetic effect. In the original language, the word for the thorns sounds almost the same as the word for the cooking-pot.
7:7: כִּי הָעֹשֶׁק יְהוֹלֵל חָכָם וִיאַבֵּד אֶת־לֵב מַתָּנָה
These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words.
Qoheleth is speaking of oppression as if it were a living thing that could drive a person out of his mind.
Here Qoheleth is speaking as if a person’s ability to judge rightly were his heart.
7:9: Qoheleth is speaking of anger as if it were a living thing that could settle down and rest in a person’s lap.
7:11: The implication is that Wisdom brings the kind of benefit that wealth brings. This could mean that wisdom is (1) as good as an inheritance or (2) good along with an inheritance.
7:12: Here Qoheleth is speaking as if the protection that wisdom and money give a person were the shadow that they cast.
Here, silver represents money and possessions in general.
Qoheleth is speaking of Wisdom as if it were a living thing that could keep alive the people who have it.
7:13: Here Qoheleth is speaking as if the way that God orders events were something that God had bent and no one could straighten.
7:14: בְּיוֹם טוֹבָה הֱיֵה בְטוֹב וּבְיוֹם רָעָה רְאֵה
Qoheleth is referring to all of the circumstances of a person’s life by naming two extremes, a day of good and a day of misfortune.
7:15: Here Qoheleth is speaking as if his lifetime were vapor, which appears for a moment and then is gone.
7:16: The implication is that Qoheleth is warning against a kind of excess, not against being righteous. This could mean: (1) being self-righteous; or (2) being excessively scrupulous about doing what is right.
7:17: Qoheleth is using the question form to warn his readers about the consequence of being wicked and foolish.

Qoheleth is using not your time as a common expression of the culture to mean “before the time when you would otherwise die.” This could mean: (1) that the person dies needlessly young because of their own foolishness; or (2) that God cuts their life short.
7:18: Here Qoheleth is speaking as if his advice were an object that a person could take hold of.
7:19: הַחָכְמָה תָּעֹז לֶחָכָם מֵעֲשָׂרָה שַׁלִּיטִים אֲשֶׁר הָיוּ בָּעִיר
Here Qoheleth is speaking as if wisdom were a defense that makes a person strong, the way that rulers defend a city.
Qoheleth says ten rulers as an extreme statement for emphasis. He means a large number of powerful officials.
7:20: אֵין צַדִּיק בָּאָרֶץ אֲשֶׁר יַעֲשֶׂה־טּוֹב וְלֹא יֶחֱטָא
Here Qoheleth uses or invents a proverb in order to state that every person sins.
7:21: The implication is that it would be especially painful to hear your servant speak badly of you, since a servant owed his master respect.
7:24: Here Qoheleth is speaking as if what he wanted to understand were Far away and deep in a place that he could not reach.
Qoheleth is using the question form to emphasize that no one is able to understand these things.
7:25: Qoheleth is speaking of his heart as if it were a living thing that could search alongside him.
The terms to know, to explore, and {to} seek mean similar things. Qoheleth is using the three terms together for emphasis.
The terms {the} wickedness {that is} folly and the foolishness {that is} madness mean similar things. Qoheleth is using the two terms together for emphasis.
7:26: Here Qoheleth is speaking as if the distress that this woman causes were a taste that was more bitter than death.
The implication is that Qoheleth is describing something that traps a man and ruins him. This could mean: (1) a seductive woman; or (2) folly, which Qoheleth pictures as a woman.
Here Qoheleth is speaking as if this woman’s intentions were nets for catching a man.
Here Qoheleth is speaking as if this woman’s hold on a man were chains.
7:28: Here, my soul represents the seeker himself.
Qoheleth says a thousand {men} as an extreme statement for emphasis. He means a very large number of people.
7:29: Here Qoheleth is speaking as if living rightly were standing upright.
8:1: מִי כְּהֶחָכָם וּמִי יוֹדֵעַ פֵּשֶׁר דָּבָר
Qoheleth is using the question form to emphasize that no one is like the wise person, because only a wise person knows the interpretation of a matter.
Here Qoheleth is speaking as if wisdom were a light that enlightens a person’s face. He means that wisdom gives a person a cheerful or gracious expression.
8:3: Here, face represents the presence of the king. This also occurs in verse 12.
8:4: Qoheleth is imagining someone using the question form to challenge or rebuke the king for what he is doing.
8:5: Here Qoheleth is speaking as if the heart of a wise person were the part of him that thinks and understands. He means the mind of a wise person.
8:7: Qoheleth is using the question form to emphasize that no one can tell a person what will happen in the future.
8:8: Qoheleth is speaking of wickedness as if it were a living thing that could deliver its masters. He means that doing wicked things will not save wicked people from death.
8:10: The implication is that while these wicked people were alive, they regularly went into and out of a place of holiness, that is, the temple.
The implication is that these wicked people had done evil deeds in the same city where people praised them.
8:11: מָלֵא לֵב בְּנֵי הָאָדָם בָּהֶם לַעֲשׂוֹת רָע
Here Qoheleth is speaking as if the heart of people were a container that fills with the desire to do evil.
8:12: Qoheleth says a hundred times as an extreme statement for emphasis. He means very many times.
8:13: The point of this comparison is that just as the shadow soon passes away, so the life of a wicked person will come to an end.
8:14: The implication is that righteous people experience what wicked people deserve for their deeds, and wicked people experience what righteous people deserve for their deeds.
8:15: Qoheleth is speaking of joy as if it were a living thing that could accompany him in his toil. He means that a person can experience joy while he works hard.
8:16: Qoheleth is referring to all of the time by naming two major components, the day and the night.
9:1: Here, to their faces represents “ahead of them,” that is, in their future.
9:2: Other ancient manuscripts read “vapor” and place that word at the end of the previous verse.

Qoheleth is referring to all kinds of people by naming pairs of major components that are opposites, such as the righteous person and the wicked person, the pure person and the unclean person, and the person who sacrifices and the person who does not sacrifice.

The implication is that the person who swears an oath is someone who makes oaths carelessly, while the person who fears an oath is someone who respects oaths so much that he is careful about making them. Qoheleth means that the same thing happens to both kinds of people.

Qoheleth is speaking as if the heart of people were a container that is full of evil and that has madness in it. He means that people constantly think about and desire evil and foolish things.

9:6: Qoheleth is speaking as if the love, hate, and jealousy of dead people were living things that have perished. He means that these feelings have ended.

Qoheleth is speaking as if the good things that people can experience in life were a portion, that is, a share of property that someone receives. He means that dead people can no longer take part in or enjoy anything that happens in this life.
9:7: Qoheleth is using Go as a common expression of the culture to mean “Come now.” He is urging people to act, not telling them to leave a place.
Qoheleth is using bread to represent food in general.

The implication is that the swift do not always win the race and the mighty do not always win the war.

Here Qoheleth uses or invents a proverb in order to show that the quiet words of wise people are more valuable than the shouting of a ruler who leads foolish people.
10:1: The point of this comparison is that just as Flies of death can spoil a whole container of a perfumer’s oil, so a little foolishness can spoil the good that wisdom and honor have accomplished. Qoheleth implies this comparison by placing the two statements next to each other.
10:2: Here Qoheleth is speaking as if a person’s mind and will were his heart. It means that what a person thinks and desires guides the way he lives.

Here Qoheleth is speaking as if the heart could turn to his right or to his left. In this culture, the right side represented strength and favor, and the left side represented weakness or misfortune. This could mean: (1) a wise person is inclined toward what is good, while a fool is inclined toward what is evil, or (2) a wise person’s understanding protects him, while a fool is exposed to harm.
10:3: Qoheleth is speaking of the fool’s lack of sense as if it were a living thing that could speak to everyone. He means that the foolish way this person behaves shows everyone that he is a fool.
10:4: Here Qoheleth is speaking as if great sins were things that could be caused to leave. It means that remaining calm can keep great sins from having their effect. This could mean: (1) staying calm will cause the ruler to overlook great offenses or (2) staying calm will keep you from committing great sins, such as rebelling against the ruler.
10:5: The point of this comparison is that just as an unintentional sin that a ruler commits causes harm even though he did not intend it, so is the misfortune that Qoheleth saw harmful.
Here, the face represents the presence of the authority. The expression means that the error comes from the ruler himself.
10:6: Here Qoheleth is speaking as if important positions were high places and unimportant positions were the lowly place. It means that foolish people are given positions of honor and authority, while rich people are given positions of little importance.
10:7: The implication is that only important and wealthy people rode horses, while slaves walked. Qoheleth is saying that the normal order of society has been reversed.
10:8: The implication is that snakes often lived in the cracks of stone walls, so a person who breaks through a wall could be bitten by a snake hiding in it.
10:10: Here, the iron represents “the axe head,” which was made of iron.
10:11: The implication is that the snake bites someone before the snake charmer has used a charm to calm it.
10:12: Here Qoheleth is speaking as if the fool’s lips could swallow him. It means that what a fool says will bring about his own ruin.
10:14: Qoheleth is using after him as a common expression of the culture.
Qoheleth is using the question form for emphasis. He means that no one can tell a person what will happen after him.
10:16: Qoheleth is speaking to a land that he knows cannot hear him. He is doing this to communicate to the people listening to him that he feels very strongly about the harm that bad rulers cause to a nation. He is using land to mean the people who live in it.
The implication is that a king who is a youth is not able to rule well.
The implication is that your princes are feasting in the morning, when they should be working to govern the land.
10:17: Here Qoheleth is speaking as if a descendant of noble people were their son. It means that the king comes from a noble family.
The implication is that the princes eat only at the proper time for meals, not early in the morning as described in the previous verse.
10:18: Qoheleth is using hands to represent the people who should be working with them.
10:19: Qoheleth is using bread to represent food in general, especially the food served at a feast.
Qoheleth is speaking of silver as if it were a living thing that could answer people. He means that money can provide everything that people need.
10:20: Here Qoheleth is speaking as if a bird of the heavens could carry the voice of a person to others. It means that what you say in private may be reported to the people you speak about in ways you would not expect.
